title: Star Maps

beats.narrativeText: The station's damaged observatory still holds a telescope angled at the sky — pointed at something the expedition never finished recording.
Star charts and positional notes survive, but only in pieces — enough to hint at what the expedition was tracking, not enough to say for certain, yet.
The learner matches the recorded star patterns to known constellations and reads through the station's own star maps.
beats.trigger: Constellations matched and star maps read

beats.narrativeText: Measuring the angles between the recorded positions turns scattered notes into something with real shape — a pattern in the sky, not just a list of coordinates.
The learner must interpret what the matched constellations and measured angles actually mean, and reconstruct what the expedition was really studying.
The reconstructed observations reveal something bigger than a single station's worth of curiosity — the expedition's scientific objectives reached far wider than anyone assumed.
The learner reflects on how much can still be learned from data that was never even finished being recorded — as long as it was recorded carefully.
The observatory hums back to life. Whatever the expedition was really working on, it's now clear their research extended far beyond the walls of Outpost Echo itself.

activities.title: Match Constellations
activities.storyContext: The damaged observatory's surviving records show star patterns nobody finished identifying.
activities.instructions: Match the recorded star patterns to known constellations, one at a time.

activities.title: Read Star Maps
activities.storyContext: The station's own star charts and positional notes are the closest thing to a direct clue about what the expedition had been tracking.
activities.instructions: Read the station's star maps carefully and note down the exact positions the expedition recorded.
activities.output: Notes on the recorded star positions.

activities.title: Measure Angles
activities.storyContext: Scattered on their own, the recorded positions don't mean much — measured against each other, they may form a genuine pattern in the sky.
activities.instructions: Using the star chart, measure the angles between the recorded star positions and record each one precisely.
activities.output: A set of measured angles between recorded positions.

activities.title: Interpret Observations
activities.storyContext: Constellations and angles are just data on their own — put together, they should finally reveal what the expedition was actually studying.
activities.instructions: Interpret the matched constellations and measured angles together to reconstruct what the expedition's observations were actually showing.
activities.output: A reconstructed set of astronomical observations.

activities.title: Create a Seasonal Star Guide
activities.storyContext: A seasonal star guide would help future Explorers use the observatory.
activities.instructions: Create a simple seasonal star guide showing constellations visible at different times of year.

activities.title: Navigating by the Night Sky
activities.storyContext: Long before modern instruments, explorers relied on the stars to find their way.
activities.instructions: Find out how explorers navigated using the night sky before modern technology.
activities.output: None required — this is an open investigation.

prompts: What do you think the expedition was studying with the observatory, and which piece of evidence made you think so?

discussionPoints: What do you think the expedition was tracking in the night sky?
How did measuring angles help you interpret the observations?
parentGuide.preparation: No special preparation required; a real star map or night sky app can enrich the experience if available.
parentGuide.assessment: Look for careful matching of constellations and observations interpreted with reasoning, not guesswork.

completionCriteria: Constellations matched, star maps read, angles measured, and observations interpreted.
